Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

content.content:
=== CONTENT_SPEC ===
# Content spec

## Audience

Mixed on purpose: athletic performance, athletic medicine, nutrition, mental health,
applied performance, sport coaches, and admin/leadership. Write
for a smart reader outside the paper's field, at about a college freshman level. If a
term needs a stats or physiology background (effect size, VO2max, ICC), explain it in a
few words or leave it out.

## The five slides

| Slide | Heading on the deck | On the slide |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `headline` | `headline`, source line, `hook`, evidence scale |
| 2 | 01 WHAT THE RESEARCHERS DID | `did.question`, `did.facts` (three across) |
| 3 | 02 WHAT THEY FOUND | `results.stats[0]` as one sentence, `results.chart` (or `results.table`) |
| 4 | 03 WHAT IT MEANS | `meaning.summary`, `meaning.roles`, level + `trust.limitations[0]` |
| 5 | 04 COACHING TAKEAWAYS | `takeaways.bullets`, `takeaways.bottom_line` bar, citation |

**Post-only fields** (Teams post and email, never on a slide): `did.bullets`,
`results.stats[1..]`, `results.bullets`, `trust.design`, `trust.sample`,
`trust.limitations[1..]`, `takeaways.question`, the full paper title. This split came
from the distill pass (2026-09-16): each slide carries one idea and one hero element,
and the detail lives where people read it at their own pace.

The Teams post and email keep the question form of the four headings.

Visual style (2026-09-16, Eric's direction, v3): every review builds a light and a dark
deck from the same content. Dark follows the "Sleep to Compete" telemetry deck
(`07_EDUCATION/TEAM EDUCATION/FOOTBALL/Education`): charcoal, faint grid, gold labels,
teal numbers, corner-bracket panels, gold bottom-line bar, with near-white body text.
Light uses Baylor green and dark gold on a paper background with the same layout.
No header or footer strip, no italics.

Fonts: **Baylor Bears Font** for display text only (section numbers and titles, slide 1
headline and label row, role names, panel labels, "Bottom line"). **Agency FB** for
everything people read closely. Bears only has A to Z, 0 to 9, space and `. : ! - #`,
so section titles are caps statements, not questions, and `headline` must use only
those characters. build.js falls back to Agency FB bold for any display string with
another character.

The Teams post and email use the same four headings, in the same order.

## Field rules

`build.js` enforces the length limits. The judgment rules below are not machine-checked.

Slide-facing limits are tight on purpose because the type is large: `hook` 120,
`did.question` 90, `did.facts[].value` 26, `meaning.summary` 110, `meaning.roles[].line` 70,
`takeaways.bullets` 60, `takeaways.bottom_line` 55. Write these first, short, then put the
nuance in the post-only fields. Where a number in the list below disagrees, the
validator in build.js is the authority.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Weekly workflow

One paper in, one review out: a dark deck, a light deck, a Teams post, and an email,
all generated from the same `review.json`. Steps run in order; do not skip the QA gate.
The `/research-in-5` skill starts this workflow from any folder.

## 1. Intake

Eric hands over the paper one of three ways:

| Input | How to read it |
|---|---|
| PDF in `_DRIVE/07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5/_Inbox/` or a path | Read the full text, page by page. Best source. |
| DOI or URL | Fetch the article page. Articles in press often have no public PDF. If the full text is out of reach, ask Eric for the PDF; set `paper.full_text: false` and build from the abstract only as a last resort. |
| Zotero item (title, key, or tag) | `sync_zotero_library` with `include_fulltext: true`, then `search_papers` for the key, `get_paper` to confirm a PDF attachment, and `get_paper_pages` for page-located text. A just-attached PDF is not searchable until that sync runs. |

## 2. Set up the folder

- Number = highest existing `reviews/NNN_*` + 1 (`000_sample` does not count).
- Create `reviews/NNN_slug/` (slug: 2-4 lowercase words, e.g. `sleep-extension-sprint`).
- Copy `templates/review.template.json` to `reviews/NNN_slug/review.json`.

## 3. Extract to notes.md

Before writing anything for the audience, write `reviews/NNN_slug/notes.md`:

- Citation (authors, year, title, journal, DOI)
- Research question or aim, in the authors' words, with page
- Design, participants (n, sex, sport, level), duration, what was measured
- Main results: every number you might use, with page, copied from the tables as reported
- Limitations the authors state, plus any obvious ones they did not (label those "ours")
- Anything inside the paper that does not add up (a conclusion stronger than its own limitations section, a mislabeled table), and which source you used

Every number in review.json must appear here with a page number. This is what makes
the review defensible when a coach or physician asks "where did that come from?"
Never display a number you computed (a difference, a percent change); plot and
tabulate the reported values.

## 4. Write review.json

Follow `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. Set `date` to the planned send date.

Write in this order, because the slides and the post use different fields:

1. **Slide fields, short.** `headline`, `hook`, `did.question`, `did.facts`,
   `results.stats[0]`, `results.chart` (or `results.table`), `meaning.summary`,
   `meaning.roles`, `trust.level` and `trust.limitations[0]`, `takeaways.bullets`,
   `takeaways.bottom_line`. These are set in large type; build.js enforces tight limits.
2. **Post-only fields, with the nuance.** `did.bullets`, the other `results.stats`,
   `results.bullets`, `trust.design`, `trust.sample`, the other limitations,
   `takeaways.question`. These appear in the Teams post and email, never on a slide.
3. **Humanizer pass** on all audience copy (the `humanizer` skill). Keep every
   number, page, and limit; cut rule-of-three lists, "not X, but Y" lines, and stacked
   rhetorical questions.

## 5. Build and QA locally

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive
```

build.js validates first and stops on length, dash, department-name, or Baylor Bears
character errors. Fix the wording and rerun. It then writes both decks and the posts
to `build/NNN_slug/`, and publish.ps1 exports each deck to PDF and slide images.

Read all ten images, `dark-slide1.png` to `dark-slide5.png` and `light-slide1.png` to
`light-slide5.png`, and check:

- No text overflow, clipping, or overlap in either theme
- Every number on the slides matches notes.md and has a page (chart values match the paper's table)
- Slide 1 headline sits on one line; evidence scale matches the rubric
- Role lines are concrete, use department names, and only cover roles the paper touches
- Slide 5 has three takeaways and the Bottom line bar
- publish.ps1 prints `Agency FB embedded: True` for both PDFs. If False, recipients see a substitute font; do not send. "Calibri" inside the PDF is expected: it is the hidden text layer PowerPoint adds to Baylor Bears text
- `teams[_vN].md` and `email[_vN].txt` read cleanly and carry the detail the slides left out

Report PASS, FAIL (theme, slide numbers, and defects), or DEGRADED (PowerPoint export
unavailable, so slides were not visually checked). Do not call a DEGRADED review ready.
PDF export needs PowerPoint on Windows; on the Mac, `node tools/build.js` still builds
the pptx files and posts.

// index.js - rebuild the running index of past reviews.
//
//   node tools/index.js
//
// Scans reviews/*/review.json (number >= 1; #000 is the sample) and writes:
//   reviews/INDEX.md                  committed, for the repo
//   build/Research_in_5_Index.csv     copied to Drive by publish.ps1, opens in Excel

const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");
const { citation } = require("./build.js");

const root = path.join(__dirname, "..");
const reviewsDir = path.join(root, "reviews");

const rows = fs.readdirSync(reviewsDir, { withFileTypes: true })
  .filter((d) => d.isDirectory() && fs.existsSync(path.join(reviewsDir, d.name, "review.json")))
  .map((d) => JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(reviewsDir, d.name, "review.json"), "utf8")))
  .filter((r) => r.number >= 1)
  .sort((a, b) => a.number - b.number);

const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(3, "0");
const link = (r) => (r.paper.doi ? `https://doi.org/${r.paper.doi}` : r.paper.url);
const md = (s) => String(s).replace(/\|/g, "\\|");

const mdLines = [
  "# Research in 5: index",
  "",
  "Generated by `node tools/index.js`. Do not edit by hand.",
  "",
  "| # | Date | Topic | Paper | Evidence | Top takeaway |",
  "|---|---|---|---|---|---|",
  ...rows.map((r) => `| ${pad(r.number)} | ${r.date} | ${md(r.topic)} | [${md(r.paper.title)}](${link(r)}) (${md(r.paper.authors)}, ${r.paper.year}) | ${r.trust.level} | ${md(r.takeaways.bullets[0])} |`),
  "",
];
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(reviewsDir, "INDEX.md"), mdLines.join("\n"));

const csv = (s) => `"${String(s ?? "").replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;
const header = ["Number", "Date", "Topic", "Title", "Authors", "Journal", "Year", "Evidence", "Design", "Sample", "Takeaway 1", "Takeaway 2", "Takeaway 3", "Tags", "Link", "Citation"];
const csvLines = [header.map(csv).join(",")].concat(rows.map((r) => [
  pad(r.number), r.date, r.topic, r.paper.title, r.paper.authors, r.paper.journal, r.paper.year,
  r.trust.level, r.trust.design, r.trust.sample,
  r.takeaways.bullets[0], r.takeaways.bullets[1], r.takeaways.bullets[2],
  (r.tags || []).join("; "), link(r), citation(r),
].map(csv).join(",")));
fs.mkdirSync(path.join(root, "build"), { recursive: true });
// BOM so Excel reads UTF-8 correctly.
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(root, "build", "Research_in_5_Index.csv"), "﻿" + csvLines.join("\r\n") + "\r\n");

console.log(`Indexed ${rows.length} review(s).`);
=== NOTES ===
# Notes: #001 alignment and jumper's knee

Source: full text, Article in Press version (11 PDF pages). Zotero item ZEMKG5EA,
attachment CRBHKMDX (`G:\My Drive\Zotero_PDFs\Saraee et al. - 2026 - ...pdf`), tag
"Research in 5". Page numbers below are PDF pages. First draft (2026-09-16) was built
from the abstract only; rebuilt from full text the same day.

## Citation
Saraee D, Piri H, Sheikhhoseini R, Hajizadeh R (2026). Comparison of lower limb
alignment in knees with and without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball
players: a cross-sectional study. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research.
doi:10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w. Received 28 Jul 2026, accepted 3 Sep 2026 (p.1).
License CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (p.9).

## Aim
- "determine whether lower-limb alignment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar tendinopathy" (p.2)

## Design and participants
- Cross-sectional, STROBE reported (p.3)
- Elite male volleyball players from clubs in Alborz Province, Iran; purposive sampling; recruited 2025-05-22 to 2025-08-23 (p.3)
- Inclusion: unilateral PT by RLHT, male, age 18-30, consent. Exclusion: severe spinal abnormality (New York test), lower-extremity surgery history, bilateral PT (p.3)
- n = 22 from G*Power, paired t-test, effect size 0.55, alpha 0.05, power 0.80 (p.3)
- Age 19.59 +/- 2.04 y; height 191.68 +/- 6.72 cm; weight 80.59 +/- 9.02 kg; BMI 22.24 +/- 1.88 (p.3; Table 1 p.5)
- RLHT: supine palpation of tendon, tenderness reduced with knee flexed to 90 deg; reported sensitivity 88%, specificity 98%; each knee tested separately; positive = affected (p.3)
- Full-length bilateral weight-bearing AP radiographs, standardized foot position (about 8-10 deg external rotation) (p.4)
- 7 coronal angles: aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, mLDTA (p.4)
- One experienced examiner, blinded to affected/unaffected status (p.4)
- Paired t-tests, SPSS 26, alpha 0.05 (p.4)
- So the comparison is WITHIN player: painful knee vs the same player's pain-free knee (p.2, p.3, p.6 "within the same individuals")

## Results (Table 3, p.6; affected vs unaffected, mean +/- SD, p)
| Angle | Affected | Unaffected | Diff | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aLDFA | 83.89 +/- 1.78 | 83.17 +/- 2.39 | 0.72 | 0.277 |
| aTFA | 176.25 +/- 2.73 | 175.64 +/- 2.49 | 0.61 | 0.252 |
| aMPTA | 88.00 +/- 2.62 | 87.50 +/- 2.93 | 0.50 | 0.456 |
| aLDTA | 87.73 +/- 2.33 | 86.89 +/- 2.49 | 0.84 | 0.130 |
| mLDFA | 88.59 +/- 2.52 | 88.48 +/- 2.24 | 0.11 | 0.883 |
| mMPTA | 87.03 +/- 2.24 | 87.06 +/- 2.16 | 0.03 | 0.948 |
| mLDTA | 87.92 +/- 1.59 | 87.18 +/- 1.88 | 0.74 | 0.107 |

- Differences are simple subtraction of the table means (ours), used only to support "under 1 degree"; the authors say the same in words: distal femoral angles differed by less than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6 deg (p.6)
- "p-values ranged from 0.107 to 0.948" (p.6)
- 0 of 7 angles significant (p.5-6)

## Authors' interpretation
- Static coronal alignment not significantly associated with PT in this cohort (p.6)
- Tendon load is driven by dynamic factors (landing knee flexion, loading rate, muscle activation); points to training load, jump-landing mechanics, strength, tendon monitoring (p.6-7). These were NOT measured in this study.
- Future work: sagittal and transverse planes, dynamic imaging, longitudinal designs (p.7-8)

## Limitations
- Authors: did not account for prior injury, weekly training load and intensity, limb dominance, foot arch (p.7)
- Authors: elite men from one province, narrow age range; limits generalizing to women, non-elite, other sports (p.7-8)
- Authors: static radiographs; coronal plane only (p.8)
- Authors: small sample, possible Type II error; absence of difference "should not be taken as definitive evidence that no association exists" (p.8)
- Authors: no intra- or inter-rater reliability testing (p.8)
- Authors: RLHT only, no ultrasound or MRI confirmation (p.8)
- Authors: cross-sectional; longitudinal preferred (p.8)
- Ours: within-player design cannot tell whether players who get PT have different alignment from players who do not
- Ours: power calc targets a moderate effect (0.55); side-to-side gaps here were all under 1 degree
- Ours: conclusion wording (p.8, "is not associated") is stronger than the limitations section on the same page; the review follows the cautious version
- Ours: Table 2 (p.5) is captioned as the Shapiro-Wilk normality test but lists means with p-values that differ from Table 3; used Table 3 for all numbers

attachment CRBHKMDX (`G:\My Drive\Zotero_PDFs\Saraee et al. - 2026 - ...pdf`), tag
"Research in 5". Page numbers below are PDF pages. First draft (2026-09-16) was built
from the abstract only; rebuilt from full text the same day.

## Citation
Saraee D, Piri H, Sheikhhoseini R, Hajizadeh R (2026). Comparison of lower limb
alignment in knees with and without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball
players: a cross-sectional study. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research.
doi:10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w. Received 28 Jul 2026, accepted 3 Sep 2026 (p.1).
License CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (p.9).

## Aim
- "determine whether lower-limb alignment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar tendinopathy" (p.2)

## Design and participants
- Cross-sectional, STROBE reported (p.3)
- Elite male volleyball players from clubs in Alborz Province, Iran; purposive sampling; recruited 2025-05-22 to 2025-08-23 (p.3)
- Inclusion: unilateral PT by RLHT, male, age 18-30, consent. Exclusion: severe spinal abnormality (New York test), lower-extremity surgery history, bilateral PT (p.3)
- n = 22 from G*Power, paired t-test, effect size 0.55, alpha 0.05, power 0.80 (p.3)
- Age 19.59 +/- 2.04 y; height 191.68 +/- 6.72 cm; weight 80.59 +/- 9.02 kg; BMI 22.24 +/- 1.88 (p.3; Table 1 p.5)
- RLHT: supine palpation of tendon, tenderness reduced with knee flexed to 90 deg; reported sensitivity 88%, specificity 98%; each knee tested separately; positive = affected (p.3)
- Full-length bilateral weight-bearing AP radiographs, standardized foot position (about 8-10 deg external rotation) (p.4)
- 7 coronal angles: aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, mLDTA (p.4)
- One experienced examiner, blinded to affected/unaffected status (p.4)
- Paired t-tests, SPSS 26, alpha 0.05 (p.4)
- So the comparison is WITHIN player: painful knee vs the same player's pain-free knee (p.2, p.3, p.6 "within the same individuals")

## Results (Table 3, p.6; affected vs unaffected, mean +/- SD, p)
| Angle | Affected | Unaffected | Diff | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aLDFA | 83.89 +/- 1.78 | 83.17 +/- 2.39 | 0.72 | 0.277 |
| aTFA | 176.25 +/- 2.73 | 175.64 +/- 2.49 | 0.61 | 0.252 |
| aMPTA | 88.00 +/- 2.62 | 87.50 +/- 2.93 | 0.50 | 0.456 |
| aLDTA | 87.73 +/- 2.33 | 86.89 +/- 2.49 | 0.84 | 0.130 |
| mLDFA | 88.59 +/- 2.52 | 88.48 +/- 2.24 | 0.11 | 0.883 |
| mMPTA | 87.03 +/- 2.24 | 87.06 +/- 2.16 | 0.03 | 0.948 |
| mLDTA | 87.92 +/- 1.59 | 87.18 +/- 1.88 | 0.74 | 0.107 |

- Differences are simple subtraction of the table means (ours), used only to support "under 1 degree"; the authors say the same in words: distal femoral angles differed by less than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6 deg (p.6)
- "p-values ranged from 0.107 to 0.948" (p.6)
- 0 of 7 angles significant (p.5-6)

## Authors' interpretation
- Static coronal alignment not significantly associated with PT in this cohort (p.6)
- Tendon load is driven by dynamic factors (landing knee flexion, loading rate, muscle activation); points to training load, jump-landing mechanics, strength, tendon monitoring (p.6-7). These were NOT measured in this study.
- Future work: sagittal and transverse planes, dynamic imaging, longitudinal designs (p.7-8)

## Limitations
- Authors: did not account for prior injury, weekly training load and intensity, limb dominance, foot arch (p.7)
- Authors: elite men from one province, narrow age range; limits generalizing to women, non-elite, other sports (p.7-8)
- Authors: static radiographs; coronal plane only (p.8)
- Authors: small sample, possible Type II error; absence of difference "should not be taken as definitive evidence that no association exists" (p.8)
- Authors: no intra- or inter-rater reliability testing (p.8)
- Authors: RLHT only, no ultrasound or MRI confirmation (p.8)
- Authors: cross-sectional; longitudinal preferred (p.8)
- Ours: within-player design cannot tell whether players who get PT have different alignment from players who do not
- Ours: power calc targets a moderate effect (0.55); side-to-side gaps here were all under 1 degree
- Ours: conclusion wording (p.8, "is not associated") is stronger than the limitations section on the same page; the review follows the cautious version
- Ours: Table 2 (p.5) is captioned as the Shapiro-Wilk normality test but lists means with p-values that differ from Table 3; used Table 3 for all numbers

input.new_string:
## The 3-slide executive readout (optional)

A second format from the same `review.json`, for when the review has to drive a
decision rather than teach: context, finding, recommendation. Add a `readout` block and
`build.js` writes `RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_readout_light.pptx` and `_readout_dark.pptx`
alongside the five-slide decks. Leave the block out and nothing changes. It is a
format, not a revision, so it does not bump `version`.

| Slide | Heading | On the slide |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 01 CONTEXT | source line, `readout.context.title`, `readout.context.bullets`, evidence scale + `trust.design`/`trust.sample` |
| 2 | 02 FINDING | `readout.finding.title`, `results.chart`, `readout.finding.bullets`, citation |
| 3 | 03 RECOMMENDATION | `readout.recommendation.title`, then Action, Confidence and risk, Validation, then the bottom-line bar |

- **context.title** (110): the decision as a question, in one line. Not the paper's aim.
- **context.bullets** (2-4, 105 each): what we looked at, and the constraints the
  decision lives inside. No background and no motivation: the hook stays off this deck.
- **finding.title** (95): an action title that states the result, not the topic.
  "Both knees line up the same: 0 of 7 angles differed", not "Alignment results".
- **finding.bullets** (2-3, 115 each): the facts that back the title, each with a page.
- **recommendation.title** (95): the ask, in one line.
- **recommendation.action / .confidence / .validation** (200 each): what to do, how sure
  we are and what could be wrong, and how we will know. All three are required. Drop one
  and the slide goes back to being a report that hands the decision to the room.

The evidence rubric still binds the verb: Preliminary recommends a pilot or a watch, not
a "do". `results.chart` is required, because slide 2 is one chart plus three bullets.

Titles are set in Agency FB, not Baylor Bears, because action titles need `?` and `,`.
Only the section row is Bears.

## Evidence level rubric

# Content spec

## Audience

Mixed on purpose: athletic performance, athletic medicine, nutrition, mental health,
applied performance, sport coaches, and admin/leadership. Write
for a smart reader outside the paper's field, at about a college freshman level. If a
term needs a stats or physiology background (effect size, VO2max, ICC), explain it in a
few words or leave it out.

## The five slides

| Slide | Heading on the deck | On the slide |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `headline` | `headline`, source line, `hook`, evidence scale |
| 2 | 01 WHAT THE RESEARCHERS DID | `did.question`, `did.facts` (three across) |
| 3 | 02 WHAT THEY FOUND | `results.stats[0]` as one sentence, `results.chart` (or `results.table`) |
| 4 | 03 WHAT IT MEANS | `meaning.summary`, `meaning.roles`, level + `trust.limitations[0]` |
| 5 | 04 COACHING TAKEAWAYS | `takeaways.bullets`, `takeaways.bottom_line` bar, citation |

**Post-only fields** (Teams post and email, never on a slide): `did.bullets`,
`results.stats[1..]`, `results.bullets`, `trust.design`, `trust.sample`,
`trust.limitations[1..]`, `takeaways.question`, the full paper title. This split came
from the distill pass (2026-09-16): each slide carries one idea and one hero element,
and the detail lives where people read it at their own pace.

The Teams post and email keep the question form of the four headings.

Visual style (2026-09-16, Eric's direction, v3): every review builds a light and a dark
deck from the same content. Dark follows the "Sleep to Compete" telemetry deck
(`07_EDUCATION/TEAM EDUCATION/FOOTBALL/Education`): charcoal, faint grid, gold labels,
teal numbers, corner-bracket panels, gold bottom-line bar, with near-white body text.
Light uses Baylor green and dark gold on a paper background with the same layout.
No header or footer strip, no italics.

Fonts: **Baylor Bears Font** for display text only (section numbers and titles, slide 1
headline and label row, role names, panel labels, "Bottom line"). **Agency FB** for
everything people read closely. Bears only has A to Z, 0 to 9, space and `. : ! - #`,
so section titles are caps statements, not questions, and `headline` must use only
those characters. build.js falls back to Agency FB bold for any display string with
another character.

The Teams post and email use the same four headings, in the same order.

## Field rules

`build.js` enforces the length limits. The judgment rules below are not machine-checked.

Slide-facing limits are tight on purpose because the type is large: `hook` 120,
`did.question` 90, `did.facts[].value` 26, `meaning.summary` 110, `meaning.roles[].line` 70,
`takeaways.bullets` 60, `takeaways.bottom_line` 55. Write these first, short, then put the
nuance in the post-only fields. Where a number in the list below disagrees, the
validator in build.js is the authority.

- **headline** (26, Bears characters only): the big slide 1 line. A short noun phrase for the question the paper tests, e.g. `Alignment vs tendon pain`, `Sleep extension`.
- **takeaways.bottom_line** (80): one sentence for the gold bar. The single thing to remember.
- **results.chart** (optional, preferred when the paper reports mean ± SD for two conditions): `title` (Bears-friendly), `a_label`, `b_label`, `unit`, `rows` of `{ label, a: [mean, sd], b: [mean, sd] }` copied from the paper, `source`. Drawn as dot + ±1 SD bar per row, each row centered on its own midpoint so different scales can share a panel. When present it replaces the table on slide 3.
- **hook** (150): why a coach should spend five minutes on this. A tension or a practical question, not a restatement of the title.
- **did.question** (170): the aim in plain language, not the authors' jargon.
- **did.bullets** (2-4, 115 each): what they actually did, in order. Who, what, how long, how measured.
- **did.facts** (2-3): short label/value pairs. Usually Design, Who, Measured.
- **results.stats** (1-3): the headline numbers. `value` is 8 characters max (`+9%`, `2.1x`, `-0.4 s`, `No change`). `label` says what it means. `page` is required in practice. Report numbers exactly as the paper does; never compute new ones.
- **results.table** (optional, strongly preferred): the paper's main results table, trimmed. `columns` 3-5, `rows` 1-8, every cell 22 characters max, copied exactly from the paper (mean ± SD, p). `source` names the table and page. Give jargon measures a plain gloss in the first column (`aLDFA, distal femur`).
- **results.bullets** (1-3, 140 each): the results in words, including null results. A "no difference" finding is a finding.
- **meaning.summary** (200): the so-what in one or two sentences.
- **meaning.roles** (2-4): one concrete line per role the paper touches. Pick from: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance, Nutrition, Mental Health, Sport Coaches, Leadership. Skip a role rather than stretch to fit it. These are Baylor's department names (Eric, 2026-09-16): Athletic Performance, not strength and conditioning; Athletic Medicine, not sports medicine; Applied Performance, not sport science. build.js rejects any other role name.
- **takeaways.bullets** (2-3, 110 each): things a coach or staff member could do or watch for. Match the verb to the evidence: Strong can say "do", Moderate says "consider", Preliminary says "watch" or "pilot".
- **takeaways.question** (150): an open question about our own practice that invites replies in the Teams thread. Not a quiz question.
- **trust**: see the rubric below. `limitations` (1-3, 70 each) are the ones that matter most for our athletes.

## Evidence level rubric

| Level | Typical study |
|---|---|
| **Strong** | Systematic review or meta-analysis; or a large, well-controlled randomized trial in athletes similar to ours. |
| **Moderate** | Randomized or controlled trial with a small sample; or a large prospective cohort in athletes. |
| **Preliminary** | Pilot or case series; cross-sectional snapshot; non-athlete or very different population; abstract-only review; industry-funded without independent replication. |

When in doubt between two levels, pick the lower one and say why in `limitations`.

## Writing rules

- No em dashes or en dashes (the validator rejects them). Use a comma, a colon, or a new sentence.
- No hype: "groundbreaking", "game-changer", "proves", "revolutionary".
- Correlation is not causation. Observational studies "found a link", they do not "show that X causes Y".
- Lead with the answer. Short sentences.

A second deck format from the same `review.json`: **Context, Finding, Recommendation**. For when a review has to drive a decision rather than teach.

Built from the 3-slide executive readout pattern Eric came across: slide 1 sets up the question and the constraints, slide 2 is one chart with an action title plus three bullets, slide 3 is a specific recommendation with its confidence, its risk, and a validation plan.

## How it works

Add a `readout` block to `review.json` and `build.js` also writes `_readout_dark.pptx` and `_readout_light.pptx`. Leave the block out and nothing changes. It is a format, not a revision, so it does not bump `version`.

Manifest theme keys are `readout-dark` / `readout-light`, because `publish.ps1` names QA images `<theme>-slideN.png` and the five-slide images would otherwise be overwritten. No change to `publish.ps1` was needed.

## The refactor

Drawing primitives moved into `makeDraw(pres, th)` so both formats render from one definition of the look: `slide`, `panel`, `rule`, `display`, `sectionHead`, `evidenceScale`, `chart`. The five-slide deck is unchanged; the regenerated slide images confirm it. The chart helper takes a `values` flag, since the readout drops the value column: on that slide the overlap is the message.

## Constraints handled

- Action titles need `?` and `,`, which Baylor Bears lacks, so readout titles are Agency FB. Only the section row is Bears, which keeps the series look without a silent font fallback.
- The citation sits under the chart on slide 2, so nothing collides with the bottom-line bar on slide 3.
- The evidence rubric still binds the verb: Preliminary recommends a pilot, not a "do".
- `results.chart` is required when a readout is present, since slide 2 is one chart plus three bullets.

## QA

`pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/001_alignment-jumpers-knee -NoDrive` on #001 v4. All six readout slides read in both themes: no overflow, clipping, or overlap. Every number traces to `notes.md` with a page. `Agency FB embedded: True` on all four PDFs. Not copied to Drive.

The five-slide deck is staff education. The readout names an owner and asks for a decision, and the compression forces a recommendation the paper only weakly supports. Worth deciding whether the readout is a per-paper option, a replacement, or a one-off before it becomes the series default.

EOF

entries.name: SendUserFile
entries.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

=== AGENTS.md ===
# AGENTS.md

Project: Weekly_Research_Review

## What this is
"Research in 5": a weekly review of one research paper Eric picks, for Baylor
Athletics cross-functional health and wellness staff, the Applied Performance team,
and admin/leadership. Each week produces a 5-slide Baylor-branded deck in dark and light
themes (the dark PDF is posted in the MS Teams channel), a Teams post, and a plain-text
email for training staff outside Teams. Every review answers the same four questions: What did the researchers do? What
were the results? What does this mean? What are the coaching takeaways? It also rates how
much to trust the paper. A running index keeps past reviews searchable.

Eric supplies the paper: a PDF, a DOI or URL, or a Zotero item.

## How to run a review
Follow `docs/WORKFLOW.md` step by step. Content rules, length limits, and the
evidence-level rubric are in `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. The one-command build is:

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive   # build + QA locally
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug            # then publish to Drive
```

## Layout
| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `reviews/NNN_slug/review.json` | The review content. Source of truth for deck, post, and email. Committed. |
| `reviews/NNN_slug/notes.md` | Extraction notes with page numbers for every number used. Committed. |
| `reviews/INDEX.md` | Generated index of past reviews. Committed. |
| `templates/review.template.json` | Blank review to copy. |
| `tools/build.js` | Validates review.json, writes dark and light decks, teams.md, email.txt to `build/`. |
| `tools/index.js` | Rebuilds INDEX.md and the Drive index CSV. |
| `tools/publish.ps1` | build, PowerPoint export to PDF and PNGs, index, copy to Drive. |
| `build/` | Local outputs. Gitignored. |

Drive: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\07_EDUCATION\Research_in_5\`
(`_DRIVE/07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5` from DEV). One folder per review holds the dark and
light pptx and pdf, teams.md, email.txt (with `_vN` suffixes for revisions), and the
paper PDF. `_Inbox/` is where Eric drops new papers.
`Research_in_5_Index.csv` at the top is the staff-facing index.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- Paper PDFs never go in git (copyright). They live in the Drive review folder.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.
- Never invent or compute a number. Every figure in a review traces to a page in the paper.

content.text:
**Hook failures from session start**, which I should have surfaced first: `daily-backup` reported 1 error on `repo-push:dotclaude` (log at `~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`), and `memsearch-sync` hit `index ETIMEDOUT` 7x consecutively — Docker Desktop hosts Milvus, so check it's running.

**Sanity check:** `build.js` validation passes; I read all six readout slides (dark + light) and re-read all three after the copy fix — no overflow, clipping, or overlap; `Agency FB embedded: True` on all four PDFs; every number traces to `notes.md` with a page. I also regression-checked the existing 5-slide deck (slides 1, 3, 5) since I refactored shared drawing code — it renders identically to v4.

## What I built

#001 compressed to Context / Finding / Recommendation, in the same v4 telemetry aesthetic — same charcoal + gold + teal, Bears section rows, corner-bracket panels, gold bottom-line bar. Dark and light twins, as the series always builds.

It's an **optional second format**, not a revision: add a `readout` block to `review.json` and `build.js` writes `_readout_dark/_light` alongside the five-slide decks. Leave it out and nothing changes. Version stays 4.

## What got cut, and why

| Cut | Why |
|---|---|
| `hook` | The article is explicit: no motivation, no framing. Just the question. |
| `did.facts` three-across | Folded into context bullets as constraints. |

**Sanity check:** rebuilt after the fixes, re-read all three readout slides in both themes (no overflow or clipping), `Agency FB embedded: True` on all four PDFs, committed and pushed to PR #7.

Codex returned FAIL with five findings. Four held and I fixed them:

- **Verb strength.** "Skip" / "Do not add" are do-level instructions against a Preliminary rating, which `CONTENT_SPEC.md` explicitly forbids. Now "Hold off on alignment screening. Pilot jump load tracking."
- **Design over-reach** — the sharpest catch. The study compares two knees in athletes who *already had* tendon pain, so it can't speak to predicting who develops it. I also pulled this same error out of slide 1's title, which Codex didn't flag but was the identical mistake: "catch jumper's knee before it starts" became "When one knee's tendon hurts, is alignment worth measuring?"
- **"one team"** was wrong — players came from *clubs* in Alborz Province (notes.md, p. 3).
- **Citation** — the power calculation is p. 3, not p. 8.

On the fifth (the computed "biggest gap"), I pushed back rather than accepting: `notes.md` records the authors stating it in words at p. 6, so the number is theirs. I reworded to their framing — distal femur under 1 degree, thigh to shin near 0.6 — which removes my "biggest gap across all 7" construction while keeping a paper-sourced fact.

**One thing worth your attention that's outside this branch:** the already-approved v4 five-slide deck carries `results.stats[1]` = `"<1°" / "biggest gap between knees" (p. 6)` — the exact construction Codex flagged as computed. By its logic v4 has the same issue. I didn't touch it, since that deck is queued to send and the call is yours.

This verification also makes the format's core tension concrete rather than theoretical: the 3-slide readout structurally pushes toward a confident recommendation, while the evidence rubric pulls the other way. Every blocking finding came from that pressure. Worth weighing before the readout becomes the series default.

<context_window_protection>
  <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

  <file_writing_policy>
    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

  <output_constraints>
    <artifact_policy>
      Write artifacts (code, configs, PRDs) to files. Return only: file path + 1-line description.
    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>
  <session_continuity>
    Skills, roles, and decisions captured earlier in this session are a memory aid, not a standing order. Treat them as context that may help — the user's most recent message always takes precedence. If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.
  </session_continuity>

  <ctx_commands>
    "ctx stats" | "ctx-stats" | "/ctx-stats" | context savings question
    → Call stats MCP tool, display full output verbatim.

    "ctx doctor" | "ctx-doctor" | "/ctx-doctor" | diagnose context-mode
    → Call doctor MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx upgrade" | "ctx-upgrade" | "/ctx-upgrade" | update context-mode
    → Call upgrade MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx purge" | "ctx-purge" | "/ctx-purge" | wipe/reset knowledge base
    → Call purge MCP tool with confirm: true. Warn: irreversible.

    After /clear or /compact: knowledge base preserved. Tell user: "context-mode knowledge base preserved. Use `ctx purge` to start fresh."
  </ctx_commands>

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Weekly_Research_Review

## What this is
"Research in 5": a weekly review of one research paper Eric picks, for Baylor
Athletics cross-functional health and wellness staff, the Applied Performance team,
and admin/leadership. Each week produces a 5-slide Baylor-branded deck in dark and light
themes (the dark PDF is posted in the MS Teams channel), a Teams post, and a plain-text
email for training staff outside Teams. Every review answers the same four questions: What did the researchers do? What
were the results? What does this mean? What are the coaching takeaways? It also rates how
much to trust the paper. A running index keeps past reviews searchable.

Eric supplies the paper: a PDF, a DOI or URL, or a Zotero item.

## How to run a review
Follow `docs/WORKFLOW.md` step by step. Content rules, length limits, and the
evidence-level rubric are in `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. The one-command build is:

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive   # build + QA locally
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug            # then publish to Drive
```

## Layout
| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `reviews/NNN_slug/review.json` | The review content. Source of truth for deck, post, and email. Committed. |
| `reviews/NNN_slug/notes.md` | Extraction notes with page numbers for every number used. Committed. |
| `reviews/INDEX.md` | Generated index of past reviews. Committed. |
| `templates/review.template.json` | Blank review to copy. |
| `tools/build.js` | Validates review.json, writes dark and light decks, teams.md, email.txt to `build/`. |
| `tools/index.js` | Rebuilds INDEX.md and the Drive index CSV. |
| `tools/publish.ps1` | build, PowerPoint export to PDF and PNGs, index, copy to Drive. |
| `build/` | Local outputs. Gitignored. |

Drive: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\07_EDUCATION\Research_in_5\`
(`_DRIVE/07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5` from DEV). One folder per review holds the dark and

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

input.content:
# 2026-09-18: the 3-slide executive readout

## What this was

Eric read an article on the "3-Slide Executive Readout" (Context, Finding,
Recommendation) and asked what #001 would look like compressed to that shape, in
the same aesthetic as the current v4 dark deck. The output is an optional second
deck format built from the same `review.json`, not a replacement for the weekly
five-slide review.

Branch `worktree-three-slide-readout`, draft **PR #7**. Four commits.

## How it works

Add a `readout` block to `review.json` and `build.js` writes two more decks
alongside the usual pair:

```
RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_readout_dark.pptx
RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_readout_light.pptx
```

Leave the block out and nothing changes. It is a **format, not a revision**, so it
does not bump `version`. #001 stays v4 and gains `_readout_` files next to the
existing ones.

Slide map:

| Slide | Content |
|---|---|
| 01 CONTEXT | source line, `readout.context.title`, `context.bullets`, evidence scale + design/sample |
| 02 FINDING | `finding.title`, `results.chart`, `finding.bullets`, citation |
| 03 RECOMMENDATION | `recommendation.title`, then Action / Confidence and risk / Validation, then the bottom-line bar |

## Decisions and the reasoning behind them

**Manifest theme keys are `readout-dark` / `readout-light`, not `dark` / `light`.**
`publish.ps1` names QA images `<theme>-slideN.png`. Reusing the theme key would have
made the readout's slide images silently overwrite the five-slide deck's. Naming
them distinctly meant **zero changes to `publish.ps1`**. If a third format is ever
added, follow the same rule.

**Drawing primitives extracted into `makeDraw(pres, th)`.** Previously the helpers
(`slide`, `panel`, `rule`, `display`, section head, evidence scale, chart) were
closures inside `buildDeck`. Both formats now render from one definition, so the
look cannot drift between them. The five-slide deck is unchanged; all five slides
were re-read after the refactor to confirm before anything was overwritten on Drive.

**The chart helper takes a `values` flag.** The five-slide deck shows the numeric
mean column; the readout drops it. On a decision slide the *overlap* of the two
series is the message, and the numbers live in the Teams post. Same helper, so the
plot geometry cannot diverge.

**Readout titles are Agency FB, not Baylor Bears.** Action titles need `?` and `,`,
which Bears lacks. `display()` would silently fall back to Agency FB bold for the
whole string, so the fallback was made explicit instead. Only the section row
(CONTEXT / FINDING / RECOMMENDATION) is Bears, which keeps the series look.

**The citation sits on slide 2, under the chart.** First build put it on slide 3
where it collided with the gold bottom-line bar. Slide 2 is also where the numbers
it backs actually are.

## The content problem this format creates

The five-slide deck is staff education. The readout names an owner and asks for a
decision, and the format pushes toward a confident recommendation while the
evidence rubric pulls the other way. **Every defect found in review came from that
pressure.** Codex verified the finding and recommendation against `notes.md` and
returned FAIL on four counts, all fixed:

1. **Do-level verbs against a Preliminary rating.** "Skip the alignment screen",
   "Do not add". `CONTENT_SPEC.md` says Preliminary recommends a pilot or a watch.
   Now "Hold off on alignment screening. Pilot jump load tracking."
2. **Treating a within-player design as evidence about predictive screening.** The
   study compares two knees in athletes who *already had* tendon pain, so it cannot
   say who will develop it. The slide 1 title had the same error one slide earlier
   ("catch jumper's knee before it starts") and was recast to "When one knee's
   tendon hurts, is alignment worth measuring?"
3. **"one team"** was wrong. Players came from *clubs* in Alborz Province
   (`notes.md`, p. 3). Now "clubs in one Iranian province".
4. **Citation p. 8** for the power calculation, which is p. 3. Now "(p. 3, p. 8)".

An earlier self-caught error in the same family: the recommendation originally said
"volleyball and basketball", but the authors put other sports out of scope
(p. 7-8). Now "starting with volleyball".

Codex's fifth finding was **rebutted, not accepted**: it called "biggest side to
side gap under 1 degree" a computed number banned by AGENTS.md. `notes.md` records
that the authors state it in words on p. 6 ("distal femoral angles differed by less
than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6"). The number is theirs. The bullet was
reworded to their framing rather than dropped.

## Files

Created:

# 2026-09-18: the 3-slide executive readout

## What this was

Eric read an article on the "3-Slide Executive Readout" (Context, Finding,
Recommendation) and asked what #001 would look like compressed to that shape, in
the same aesthetic as the current v4 dark deck. The output is an optional second
deck format built from the same `review.json`, not a replacement for the weekly
five-slide review.

Branch `worktree-three-slide-readout`, draft **PR #7**. Four commits.

## How it works

Add a `readout` block to `review.json` and `build.js` writes two more decks
alongside the usual pair:

```
RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_readout_dark.pptx
RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_readout_light.pptx
```

Leave the block out and nothing changes. It is a **format, not a revision**, so it
does not bump `version`. #001 stays v4 and gains `_readout_` files next to the
existing ones.

Slide map:

| Slide | Content |
|---|---|
| 01 CONTEXT | source line, `readout.context.title`, `context.bullets`, evidence scale + design/sample |
| 02 FINDING | `finding.title`, `results.chart`, `finding.bullets`, citation |
| 03 RECOMMENDATION | `recommendation.title`, then Action / Confidence and risk / Validation, then the bottom-line bar |

## Decisions and the reasoning behind them

**Manifest theme keys are `readout-dark` / `readout-light`, not `dark` / `light`.**
`publish.ps1` names QA images `<theme>-slideN.png`. Reusing the theme key would have
made the readout's slide images silently overwrite the five-slide deck's. Naming
them distinctly meant **zero changes to `publish.ps1`**. If a third format is ever
added, follow the same rule.

**Drawing primitives extracted into `makeDraw(pres, th)`.** Previously the helpers
(`slide`, `panel`, `rule`, `display`, section head, evidence scale, chart) were
closures inside `buildDeck`. Both formats now render from one definition, so the
look cannot drift between them. The five-slide deck is unchanged; all five slides
were re-read after the refactor to confirm before anything was overwritten on Drive.

**The chart helper takes a `values` flag.** The five-slide deck shows the numeric
mean column; the readout drops it. On a decision slide the *overlap* of the two
series is the message, and the numbers live in the Teams post. Same helper, so the
plot geometry cannot diverge.

**Readout titles are Agency FB, not Baylor Bears.** Action titles need `?` and `,`,
which Bears lacks. `display()` would silently fall back to Agency FB bold for the
whole string, so the fallback was made explicit instead. Only the section row
(CONTEXT / FINDING / RECOMMENDATION) is Bears, which keeps the series look.

**The citation sits on slide 2, under the chart.** First build put it on slide 3
where it collided with the gold bottom-line bar. Slide 2 is also where the numbers
it backs actually are.

## The content problem this format creates

The five-slide deck is staff education. The readout names an owner and asks for a
decision, and the format pushes toward a confident recommendation while the
evidence rubric pulls the other way. **Every defect found in review came from that
pressure.** Codex verified the finding and recommendation against `notes.md` and
returned FAIL on four counts, all fixed:

1. **Do-level verbs against a Preliminary rating.** "Skip the alignment screen",
   "Do not add". `CONTENT_SPEC.md` says Preliminary recommends a pilot or a watch.
   Now "Hold off on alignment screening. Pilot jump load tracking."
2. **Treating a within-player design as evidence about predictive screening.** The
   study compares two knees in athletes who *already had* tendon pain, so it cannot
   say who will develop it. The slide 1 title had the same error one slide earlier
   ("catch jumper's knee before it starts") and was recast to "When one knee's
   tendon hurts, is alignment worth measuring?"
3. **"one team"** was wrong. Players came from *clubs* in Alborz Province
   (`notes.md`, p. 3). Now "clubs in one Iranian province".
4. **Citation p. 8** for the power calculation, which is p. 3. Now "(p. 3, p. 8)".

An earlier self-caught error in the same family: the recommendation originally said
"volleyball and basketball", but the authors put other sports out of scope
(p. 7-8). Now "starting with volleyball".

Codex's fifth finding was **rebutted, not accepted**: it called "biggest side to
side gap under 1 degree" a computed number banned by AGENTS.md. `notes.md` records
that the authors state it in words on p. 6 ("distal femoral angles differed by less
than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6"). The number is theirs. The bullet was
reworded to their framing rather than dropped.
